questions.q: How does long-term retention (LTR) relate to the 7-35 day short-term backup retention window?
options: It is a separate, independently configured policy that can retain designated backups for up to 10 years, layered on top of the short-term window
It simply extends the short-term window's default from 7 days to 35 days automatically
It replaces the short-term window entirely once enabled
It only applies to databases using geo-redundant storage
questions.explain: LTR is distinct from and independent of the operational 7-35 day short-term window — it exists for a different purpose, at a much longer horizon.

questions.q: What frequencies can a long-term retention policy be configured on?
options: Weekly, monthly, and yearly, each with its own independently set retention duration
Only daily, with no other frequency options
Only yearly, capped at exactly 10 years
Only hourly, matching transaction log backup frequency
questions.explain: The Retention policies tab lets a DBA set weekly, monthly, and yearly retention durations independently on the same database.

questions.q: Where does a DBA find and restore from existing long-term retention backups?
options: The Available backups tab, which is separate from the point-in-time restore option
The same point-in-time restore timestamp picker used for short-term backups
LTR backups cannot be restored — they exist only for auditing purposes
The server's Deleted databases list
questions.explain: LTR backups appear in their own Available backups list, distinct from the short-term point-in-time restore workflow covered in the previous lesson.

questions.q: What is the key difference between restoring from an LTR backup versus a point-in-time restore?
options: LTR gives you a specific designated backup (a particular week's, month's, or year's), while point-in-time restore lets you pick any arbitrary second within its shorter window
LTR restores overwrite the original database, while point-in-time restores create a new one
LTR restores are instantaneous, while point-in-time restores take days
There is no difference — they use the exact same restore mechanism and precision
questions.explain: Both create a new database, but LTR precision is limited to the specific backups the policy designated, not an arbitrary timestamp.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe long-term retention as a compliance tool rather than an operational recovery tool?
options: Because it exists to satisfy regulations mandating retention far beyond any realistic operational recovery need, not to fix this morning's mistake
Because LTR backups are technically incapable of being restored quickly
Because LTR only works for databases in government-regulated industries
Because operational recovery always uses full backups instead of LTR
questions.explain: A DBA configures LTR based on what compliance actually requires (financial, healthcare, audit retention rules), not based on how far back an operational incident might reach.
